newsitem.title: UK: Protein may aid HIV treatment without side-effects.
newsitem.headline: Protein may aid HIV treatment without side-effects.

text.p: Scientists said on Wednesday they had identified a protein which may help treatment of HIV, the virus that causes AIDS.

Marco Baggiolini of the University of Bern, Switzerland, and colleagues said they had found a modified protein that blocks the entry of HIV into certain types of white blood cell without the undesirable side-effects of other similar treatments.
The protein is a modified form of a natural chemokine known as RANTES.
"Chemokines or chemokine derivatives may be useful agents for the treatment of infection with HIV," the scientists said in a letter to the scientific journal Nature.
Chemokines such as RANTES are substances that cells in the immune system use to signal to each other and thus prompt action against potential invaders.

Chemokines bind themselves to cell-surface receptors, to which the HIV (human immunodeficiency) virus needs access in order to infect a cell. But the virus cannot infect a cell if the receptors are already bound to a chemokine.
The binding between chemokines and receptors does however induce inflammation and other side-effects that may in the end promote rather than inhibit viral spread.
The modified form of RANTES, though, inhibits HIV infection, but with none of these therapeutically damaging side-effects.
